You said:
Heyo I have a project where I need to create pcb for the esp8266. Because I can't afford to use the uC directly an i just want to solder on the dev board with some pin sockets. How can I do this in Kicad? Also I need to be able to control another circuit that has control pins that works like a relay. There is a com pin and three functional pins. When I short com with the functional pin then the function happens. How can I simulate that with the esp8266? I will be using a portexpander anyway, but can I just use mosfets or what?
ChatGPT said:

You can absolutely do both: (1) design a “carrier” PCB that you plug a cheap ESP8266 dev board into, and (2) electronically “short COM to a function pin” in a way that behaves like a relay contact.

1) KiCad: make a PCB that accepts an ESP8266 dev board via pin sockets

The basic idea

You don’t put an ESP8266 module footprint (ESP-12E, etc.) on your PCB. Instead, you place two socket headers (or one long header, depending on the board) that match the dev board’s pin rows, so the dev board plugs in like a daughterboard.

Steps in KiCad (schematic → PCB)

  1. Identify the exact dev board (NodeMCU, Wemos D1 mini, “ESP-01 adapter”, etc.)

    • The pin spacing + which pins are broken out varies a lot.

    • Find the board’s pinout + the distance between the two header rows (often 0.9" / 22.86 mm on NodeMCU-ish boards, but do not assume).

  2. In the schematic:

    • Add 2× “Conn_01xNN” symbols (or one, depending on your dev board).

      • Example: Connector_Generic:Conn_01x15 for a 15-pin row, etc.

    • Name the nets to match what the dev board pin does: 3V3, GND, D1, D2, RX, TX, etc.

    • This makes your schematic readable and helps you not miswire I/O that has boot constraints.

  3. Assign footprints:

    • Use standard header footprints like:

      • Connector_PinHeader_2.54mm:PinHeader_1x15_P2.54mm_Vertical

      • or …Socket_… if you want the footprint to be a socket (either works electrically; footprint mainly affects drill + courtyard).

    • If you want the dev board to plug in, your PCB usually has female sockets soldered to it, and the dev board has male pins.

  4. PCB Editor: place the two headers

    • Put both headers on the board and set the row-to-row distance to exactly match the dev board.

    • Add mounting holes or 3D-printed standoffs if you want it mechanically solid.

  5. Add outline / keepouts

    • Draw the dev board outline (on Dwgs.User) so you don’t place tall parts under it.

    • Watch out for the dev board’s USB connector overhang, reset button, etc.

Strong practical tips

  • Don’t power the dev board from “VIN/5V” unless you know what you’re doing.
    Many dev boards expect USB 5V on VIN and have their own regulator, but the behavior differs. Safer approach:

    • Provide a clean 3.3V rail and feed the dev board’s 3V3 pin (only if that pin is truly the 3.3V rail input/output on that board).

  • ESP8266 has boot strap pins (GPIO0, GPIO2, GPIO15) that must be in certain states at boot. Avoid external circuitry that drags those pins the wrong way on reset/boot.

If you tell me the exact dev board model (a link or a photo, even just the name), I can tell you the header count and the usual spacing/pin order to use.

2) “Short COM to function pin” like a relay: what to use with ESP8266 / port expander?

What you described is basically a dry-contact closure: the other device expects a floating contact that closes COM to one of the function inputs.

The big question: is COM referenced to your ESP8266 ground?

If COM and the function pins are at voltages/circuits you don’t fully control (or you want to be safe), you should treat it like you need isolation (like a real relay provides).

Best options (in order)

Option A (most “relay-like”): PhotoMOS / solid-state relay (dry contact)

Use a PhotoMOS SSR (optically isolated MOSFET output) per function line.

  • Pros: behaves very similarly to a relay contact, polarity-agnostic (many are), isolated, low leakage (depends on part), simple.

  • Cons: costs more than a transistor.

Search terms: “PhotoMOS”, “MOSFET relay”, “AQY”, “Panasonic PhotoMOS”.

Option B (cheap + truly like a switch): small signal relay

A little mechanical relay driven by a transistor.

  • Pros: exact dry contact behavior, can handle weird COM voltages.

  • Cons: bulky, coil current, clicking, wear.

Option C (often fine if grounds are common): “open drain” with transistor/MOSFET

If COM is tied to the same ground/reference and the function pins are basically logic inputs, then you can simulate closure by pulling the function pin to COM (or COM to function) using a transistor arrangement.

But: a single MOSFET does not always equal a floating contact closure, because a MOSFET usually references a source node, has body diode, etc.

If you want something closer to a “bidirectional short” without isolation, use:

Option D (best non-isolated “short these two pins”): Analog switch / crosspoint / mux

Use an analog switch IC (e.g., 74HC4066 / CD4066, or better low-voltage modern parts) to connect COM to one of several pins.

  • Pros: designed to pass signals both ways (within rails), no body diode problem like a single MOSFET, can “close a contact” electronically.

  • Cons: must stay within the IC supply rails and has some on-resistance.

For 3 functions you could use:

  • One 4-channel analog switch (e.g., 4066) and use 3 channels.

Why “just MOSFETs” can bite you

  • A MOSFET has a body diode. If COM can be at a voltage relative to the function pin that forward-biases it, you get an unintended conduction path.

  • To make a “proper” bidirectional switch with MOSFETs you typically use back-to-back MOSFETs (source-to-source) per channel, which cancels the body diode issue. That works, but it’s more parts than an analog switch.

How to drive it from ESP8266 + port expander

You said you’ll use a port expander. Common ones:

  • MCP23017 (I²C, 5V tolerant depends on supply; check datasheet)

  • PCF8574 (quasi-bidirectional, weaker control)

  • TCA9555, etc.

Most expanders can:

  • Drive an analog switch input directly (easy).

  • Drive a transistor that drives a relay coil (with a flyback diode).

A very common robust architecture

  • Port expander output → analog switch enable pin (or SSR LED input via resistor).

  • COM and function pins go only to the “switch” side.

  • ESP8266 stays electrically “hands off” from the other circuit.

What I would pick (quick recommendation)

  • If you don’t know what COM electrically is, or you want to be safe: PhotoMOS SSR or small relay.

  • If COM + function pins are definitely logic-level and share ground with you: 4066-style analog switch is usually the cleanest “electronic short”.

Tiny checklist so you don’t get burned

  • Measure (or find docs for) COM voltage range vs your ground.

  • Does the other device expect momentary closure or latched closure?

  • Any minimum/maximum closure resistance? (some circuits need very low Ω; SSR/4066 have some R_on)

If you tell me:

  1. which dev board (NodeMCU vX? Wemos D1 mini?),

  2. the voltage you see on COM relative to GND,

  3. whether COM is shared ground with your PCB,

…I can tell you exactly which of the above is appropriate and a concrete schematic snippet (values + wiring).

Ok so what I want is actually "spaced pins" I guess, so that I can just solder on the dev board that comes with holes.
ChatGPT said:

Ahhh perfect — you don’t want sockets, you want the dev board soldered directly onto your PCB like a module. That’s actually cleaner and cheaper 👍

In KiCad what you’re looking for is basically through-hole pads on 2.54 mm pitch, laid out to match the dev board’s pin rows. Think of your PCB as a “motherboard” and the ESP dev board as a big DIP component.

🧩 What this is called in PCB terms

You want to place pin header footprints without the plastic header — just plated holes you solder the dev board pins into.

So instead of:

  • adding sockets
    you

  • add rows of THT pads at the correct spacing

🛠 How to do it in KiCad

1️⃣ In the schematic

Add simple connector symbols to represent the dev board pins.

For example, if your board has 2 rows of 15 pins:

  • Add two symbols:
    Connector_Generic:Conn_01x15

Rename pins to match the dev board silkscreen:

sql
Left row:  3V3, GND, D8, D7, D6...
Right row: VIN, GND, RST, EN, 3V3...

This keeps your schematic readable and prevents wiring mistakes.

2️⃣ Assign footprints

Now the key part.

Assign each connector a footprint like:

makefile
Connector_PinHeader_2.54mm:PinHeader_1x15_P2.54mm_Vertical

That footprint is just:
✔ plated holes
✔ correct pitch
✔ nice drill size
❌ no actual header required

When assembled, you solder the dev board’s male pins straight into these holes.

3️⃣ Match the row spacing

This is the part people get wrong.

In PCB Editor:

  1. Place both 1×N headers

  2. Measure the spacing between rows on the actual dev board

    • Use calipers if possible

    • Common spacings:

      • NodeMCU: 22.86 mm (0.9")

      • Wemos D1 Mini: 25.4 mm (1.0")

    • Do not trust random forum numbers — measure

  3. In KiCad:

    • Select one header

    • Press M to move

    • Use grid = 0.1 mm or 0.5 mm

    • Set exact distance using the coordinate readout

4️⃣ Hole size (important!)

Default pin header drills are often 1.0 mm.
Some dev boards use thicker square pins.

Safe settings:

  • Drill: 1.0–1.1 mm

  • Pad diameter: 1.7–2.0 mm

You can edit this in the footprint properties if needed.

5️⃣ Add a silkscreen outline

Draw the outline of the dev board on:
F.SilkS or Dwgs.User

Mark:

  • USB connector overhang

  • Antenna keepout (ESP8266 antenna area should not have copper under it)

For the antenna area:

  • Add a copper keepout zone under the antenna end of the module for better WiFi performance.

🔌 Electrical considerations

Since you're soldering it in permanently:

✔ Break out only the pins you need
✔ Add test pads for TX/RX if you’ll ever reflash it
✔ Don’t load boot pins (GPIO0, GPIO2, GPIO15) with heavy pullups/pulldowns

💡 Pro Tip (makes life easier)

Put labels on your silkscreen like:

nginx
D1  D2  D3  D4 ...
3V3 GND RST EN ...

Future-you will be VERY grateful when debugging.

If you tell me the exact board name (like “NodeMCU v3 CH340” or “Wemos D1 Mini”), I can give you:

  • typical row spacing

  • which pins to absolutely avoid loading during boot

You want male through-hole pin headers on your PCB.

makefile

That footprint is exactly a row of 0.1" (2.54 mm) spaced pins.

You solder this to your PCB, then place the dev board on top and solder it down.

1️⃣ Count pins on each side of the dev board

Look at the ESP board and count the holes.

Examples:

BoardPins per side
NodeMCU15 + 15
Wemos D1 Mini8 + 8
ESP-12 breakoutvaries

You need one pin header footprint per row.

Add connectors:

css
Conn_01x15  → Left side pins  
Conn_01x15  → Right side pins

Rename pins to match labels on the ESP board (D0, D1, RX, TX, 3V3, GND, etc.).

3️⃣ Assign footprints

Assign:

PinHeader_1x15_P2.54mm_Vertical

These represent male headers on your board.

4️⃣ Set the row spacing (CRITICAL)

Now the mechanical alignment:

  1. Open PCB Editor

  2. Place both headers

Typical spacings:

BoardRow spacing
NodeMCU22.86 mm (0.9")
Wemos D1 Mini25.4 mm (1.0")

  • Press M

5️⃣ Pin length choice (real-world tip)

Buy long-leg male headers (sometimes called stackable or Arduino headers).

You want enough exposed pin above your PCB to:

  • go through the ESP board holes

  • still have enough length to solder

Standard headers sometimes end up too short.

ParameterGood value

Add a copper keepout zone under that section.

These headers are just wires. Your schematic nets go straight to the ESP pins.

BUT remember:

PinBoot behavior caution
GPIO0Must be HIGH at boot
GPIO2Must be HIGH at boot
GPIO15Must be LOW at boot
ENMust be HIGH

🧠 Summary

You are NOT making a socket.
You are placing male pin header footprints on 2.54 mm pitch, spaced to match the ESP dev board rows.

You said:
How can I change the pin numbers?
ChatGPT said:

Ahhh yes — this part of KiCad is confusing the first time 😄
You don’t change pin numbers in the PCB — you change them in the schematic symbol.

What you want is for the pin numbers on your connector symbol to match the physical order of pins on the ESP dev board.

🧠 Important concept

In KiCad:

ThingWhat it means
Pin numberLinks schematic pin → PCB pad number
Pin nameJust a label for humans (D1, RX, GND, etc.)

So if pad 1 on your header is the top pin physically, then schematic pin 1 must be that signal.

✅ Option 1 (Easiest): Just rename the pin names

You usually don’t need to change pin numbers — just make the numbers match the physical order, and change the names.

Steps:

  1. In Schematic Editor

  2. Hover over your connector (like Conn_01x15)

  3. Press E (Properties)

  4. Click “Edit Pins”

You’ll see something like:

NumberName
1Pin_1
2Pin_2
3Pin_3

Change the Name column:

NumberName
13V3
2GND
3D8
4D7

Now your schematic is readable, and the numbering still matches the physical header pads.

🔁 When DO you change pin numbers?

Only if the symbol numbering doesn’t match the physical order of the board.

Example:
Your ESP board pin order (top → bottom):

nginx
RST
A0
D0
D5
D6

But your symbol numbers go bottom → top. Then you must renumber.

✏️ How to change pin numbers properly

You must edit the symbol in the Symbol Editor, not just on the sheet.

Steps:

  1. In Schematic Editor
    Right-click connector → Properties → Edit Symbol in Symbol Editor

  2. In Symbol Editor:

    • Click a pin

    • Press E

    • Change Pin number

Do this for each pin so that:

Physical positionPin number
Top pin1
Next2
Next3

Save the symbol as a new symbol in your project library (don’t overwrite the default KiCad one).

🔄 Then update schematic

After saving:

  • Go back to schematic

  • Tools → Update Symbols from Library

Now your connector pin numbering matches reality.

⚠️ Super important rule

Pin numbers must match the footprint pad numbers.

For a footprint like:

PinHeader_1x15_P2.54mm_Vertical

Pads are numbered:

python-repl
1
2
3
...
15

Top to bottom.

So schematic pin 1 connects to pad 1, etc.

💡 Pro tip for ESP boards

Make pin 1 = the pin closest to the USB connector (or some obvious corner)
Then number straight down. Do the same on both sides. Makes layout and debugging WAY easier.

If you tell me your exact ESP board model, I can give you the exact pin order so you can number it once and never think about it again.

You said:
Ok I added the schematics what next how do I get the pcb layout?
ChatGPT said:

Niceee, you’re at the fun part now — turning spaghetti lines into copper 😄

Here’s the full flow from schematic → actual PCB in KiCad.

🧭 STEP 1 — Assign footprints (if you haven’t yet)

Before PCB layout, every symbol needs a physical footprint.

In Schematic Editor:

  1. Click Tools → Assign Footprints

  2. For your ESP header connectors choose:

    makefile
    Connector_PinHeader_2.54mm:PinHeader_1xN_P2.54mm_Vertical

    (N = number of pins in that row)

  3. Assign footprints to every other component too (resistors, ICs, etc.)

Click OK to save.

🔄 STEP 2 — Update PCB from schematic

Now we push the design into PCB Editor.

  1. Open PCB Editor

  2. Click Tools → Update PCB from Schematic
    (or press F8)

  3. In the dialog:

    • ✔ Re-link footprints

    • ✔ Update footprints

    • ✔ Delete footprints with no symbols (optional)

  4. Click Update PCB

💥 All your parts will appear in a pile with thin lines between pads (ratsnest lines). Those lines show what must be connected.

📐 STEP 3 — Draw the board outline

You can’t route without a board shape.

  1. In PCB Editor, select layer Edge.Cuts

  2. Use Add Graphic Line tool

  3. Draw a closed outline around where your PCB should be

No outline = manufacturer can’t make the board.

📦 STEP 4 — Place the ESP dev board headers first

These define everything else.

  1. Move parts with M

  2. Rotate with R

  3. Place the two long pin headers with the exact spacing you measured earlier

  4. Keep them near one board edge if USB or antenna must stick out

💡 Add the dev board outline on Dwgs.User to help with positioning.

🧩 STEP 5 — Arrange the rest of components

General placement logic:

Component typeWhere to place
Power partsNear power entry
Decoupling capsVERY close to IC power pins
Port expanderNear ESP pins it connects to
ConnectorsNear board edge

Try to keep airwires short and uncrossed.

🔌 STEP 6 — Set board rules (optional but good)

Go to File → Board Setup

Set:

  • Track width (start with 0.25 mm / 10 mil)

  • Via size (default is fine)

  • Clearance (0.2 mm typical)

🧵 STEP 7 — Route the traces

Now connect the pads.

  1. Press X to start routing

  2. Click a pad → follow the ratsnest line → click destination pad

  3. Right-click or double-click to finish a trace

  4. Press V while routing to drop a via and switch layers

Tips:

  • Use top layer (F.Cu) for most routing

  • Use bottom (B.Cu) when needed

  • Keep traces away from ESP antenna area

🌍 STEP 8 — Add a ground plane (recommended)

Makes routing easier and improves performance.

  1. Select Add Filled Zone

  2. Choose layer: F.Cu

  3. Net: GND

  4. Draw a big polygon around the whole board

  5. Press B to fill zones

Now all GND pads connect automatically.

🔍 STEP 9 — Run Design Rule Check

  1. Click the ladybug icon (DRC)

  2. Fix:

    • Unconnected pads

    • Clearance errors

    • Tracks too close

🖨 STEP 10 — Generate manufacturing files

When DRC is clean:

  1. File → Plot

    • Select Gerber

    • Plot all copper, silkscreen, mask, Edge.Cuts

  2. Click Generate Drill Files

Zip the files → send to PCB manufacturer.

🎯 You are DONE when:

✔ No ratsnest lines remain
✔ Ground plane filled
✔ DRC shows no errors
✔ Board outline exists

If you want, send a screenshot of your PCB layout and tell me your ESP board model — I’ll sanity-check spacing, antenna clearance, and boot pin safety before you order boards.

ChatGPT said:

Yep — here are the physical details you’ll need for putting a Wemos D1 Mini V2 - ESP8266-12F CH340-style board into your KiCad PCB:

📏 Dimensions & Pin Row Spacing

✔ Overall board size: ~34.2 mm × 25.6 mm (length × width) for classic D1 Mini boards. WEMOS Documentation+1
✔ Header row spacing (center-to-center): 22.86 mm (0.9″) — this is the distance between the two rows of pins on the D1 Mini. WEMOS Documentation+1
✔ Pin pitch: 2.54 mm (0.1″) along each row. Arduino Forum

So mechanically:

  • Your PCB should have two rows of holes spaced 22.86 mm apart.

  • Within each row, the holes are 2.54 mm apart (the standard 0.1″ header).

  • Each row has 8 holes (for 8 pins) on standard D1 Mini boards. WEMOS Documentation

That gives a total of 16 pins accessible via headers (8 per side).

🛠 How to model this in KiCad

1️⃣ Choose the right footprint

For each row put a footprint like:

makefile
Connector_PinHeader_2.54mm:PinHeader_1x08_P2.54mm_Vertical

This creates a row of 8 male pins on your PCB with standard 2.54 mm holes.

2️⃣ Set the row spacing

In the PCB editor:

  • Place one 1×8 header footprint.

  • Move the second one to exactly 22.86 mm away (center-to-center).
    You can type exact placement coordinates or use the ruler.

3️⃣ Align orientation to the D1 Mini

Draw an outline on the Dwgs.User or F.SilkS layer showing where the actual board will sit so you don’t accidentally put other components underneath it.

Include the micro-USB connector overhang if your design needs it!

4️⃣ Assign schematic pins to physical pads

Make sure in your schematic:

  • You have two connector symbols (Conn_01x08).

  • The pin numbers match the physical D1 Mini pin order going down each row.

  • Example mapping (just illustration — refer to your board’s pin labels):

    nginx
    Pin 1 → D0
Pin 2 → D1
…
Pin 8 → RX

Then update the PCB from schematic. KiCad will place 16 pads (8 + 8) ready to route from.

🧠 Helpful practical points

✅ Header holes should be 1.0 mm drill with ~2.0 mm pad diameter — these fit standard 0.1″ header pins well. fritzing forum
✅ If your D1 Mini has two rows of two sets of 8 holes (some boards break out extra pins), you can still choose the exact header footprints matching the rows you want to use. Reddit
✅ In KiCad’s PCB editor, you can label each pad with its schematic name to help route easily.

📌 Summary for Wemos D1 Mini footprint

ParameterValue
Board Size~34.2 mm × 25.6 mm WEMOS Documentation
Pin Pitch2.54 mm Arduino Forum
Row Spacing22.86 mm WEMOS Documentation
Pins per Row8 per side (total 16) WEMOS Documentation
Header Type1×08 2.54 mm male pin headers

  1. Place your new WEMOS_D1_MINI symbol

  2. Open Properties

  3. Set footprint to:

makefile
YourLibrary:WEMOS_D1_MINI_THT

🚀 STEP 4 — Update PCB

Now when you do:

Tools → Update PCB from Schematic

You get:
✨ One single “module” footprint
✨ All pins grouped
✨ Board outline visible
✨ Perfect alignment guaranteed

🎯 Why this is better

Without moduleWith module
Headers can shiftAlways aligned
Hard to visualize boardBoard outline visible
Easy to mis-number pinsOne clean symbol
Hard to reuseDrop-in reusable module
